15.content: While connected, the popup starts with a row labeled "This tab". It reads "Not controlled" for an ordinary tab, "Session research" for a controlled tab, and "Session research is working" while an action runs. The row follows the active tab.

16.content: The layer is drawn in Chrome and Firefox, on tabs the session opened and on tabs it borrowed from you. It ends when the session releases or closes the tab. While it is drawn, the page shows:

17.content: An edge glow while an action runs, fading out shortly after it finishes.

18.content: A chip in the bottom right corner with an orange dot and the session name.

19.content: The orange-dot icon as the favicon, in place of the page's own icons.

20.content: A focus frame around the element an action targets, with the action name above it: Click, Hover, Type, Select, Check, Focus, Scroll, Drag or Upload. The label moves below the element when the element sits near the top edge. The frame follows elements of the main document; while the session has an iframe selected, the page shows the glow and the chip only.

21.content: The focus frame stays for a moment after the action finishes, so a run of clicks reads as one activity instead of a flicker of frames. A navigation replaces the document, and the layer is drawn again on the new page.

22.content: The layer is one host element with a shadow root. The page's styles do not reach its parts.

23.content: It uses `pointer-events: none`, so clicks, selection and hover reach the page underneath.

24.content: It is `inert` and `aria-hidden`, so screen readers and the page's accessibility tree skip it. `read_page` returns the page text without the chip, and `snapshot` does not list the layer.

25.content: Screenshots and PDFs are taken with the layer hidden, then it reappears.

26.content: The layer carries a 75-second lease that the extension renews every 30 seconds. If the extension stops renewing it, the page removes the layer by itself and restores its own favicon, so a stopped worker or a lost debugger session leaves no markings behind.

27.content: Under **Settings**, then **Pages**, turn off **Show agent activity**. The layer disappears from every controlled tab at once and is not drawn on tabs that sessions claim later. Agents keep working, and the toolbar icon and the popup row still show which session controls the tab. Turn the switch on again to draw the layer on the tabs that are still controlled.

28.content: The layer follows the system's reduced motion and reduced transparency settings: the glow stops pulsing and the chip switches to a solid background.

30.content: How the omw daemon and the browser extension split work, and how a command reaches a tab.

39.content: Two processes make up oh-my-webbridge. The daemon `omw` is a Go binary that listens on `127.0.0.1:17373`. The extension runs inside Chrome or Firefox and drives tabs through browser APIs. Agents, the CLI and the SDK call the daemon over HTTP; the daemon calls the extension over a WebSocket.

40.content: The daemon holds state that outlives a browser window.

41.content: Authentication. Every request is checked against the token here, except `GET /ping` and `POST /pair`.

42.content: Routing. It keeps one connection per browser and sends each command to Chrome or Firefox.

43.content: Concurrency and deadlines. It admits requests, applies a timeout, and answers `busy` when a limit is reached.

44.content: Files. It writes screenshots and PDFs to the paths you give it, and reads upload files for Firefox, whose extension cannot read local files.

45.content: CDP front end. `GET /json`, `GET /json/version` and `GET /devtools/page/{tab}` present Chrome tabs to CDP clients, and `omw serve --cdp` passes `/devtools/browser` through to a native DevTools endpoint.

46.content: Session bindings, stored in `bindings.json` in the config directory.

47.content: The extension owns the browser side.

48.content: Task tabs and their tab groups, including borrowing a tab that already exists.

49.content: `snapshot` of the DOM and accessibility tree, and the `@e` references derived from one snapshot.

50.content: Input: click, hover, type, select, check, focus, scroll, drag and upload.

52.content: Firefox: WebExtension APIs. `page.js` is injected into the selected frame on demand, `webRequest` handles presets and headers, `tabs.captureTab` takes screenshots, and `userScripts.execute` runs `evaluate`.

53.content: Network entries and console records for each controlled tab.

54.content: The activity layer drawn over a controlled page.

55.content: Firefox answers some actions with `unsupported`, because its extension APIs have no equivalent. The differences are listed in Firefox.

56.content: One tab belongs to one session at a time. A session that creates tabs keeps them in its own tab group; a borrowed tab stays in your group and returns on release. A tab group is neither a cookie boundary nor a security boundary: every tab in the profile shares the same logins.

57.content: The daemon keeps at most one Chrome connection and one Firefox connection. It tells them apart by the WebSocket Origin. The extension's hello reports the browser, the browser version, and the session names the extension holds.

58.content: A command may carry a `browser` field. A session binds to a browser on its first command and keeps that binding until `close_session` succeeds. The binding is written to `bindings.json`, so after a daemon restart the session is routed back to the same browser. The next hello re-reports the session names, and stale bindings are dropped.

59.content: A session without a binding goes to Chrome when it is connected, and to Firefox otherwise. `/json/list`, `/devtools/*` and raw `cdp` need the Chrome extension; `/json/version` reports the version even with no browser connected. A second connection from the same browser is refused with 409.

60.content: Requests arrive as `POST /command` with a 2 MiB body limit, or as frames on the extension WebSocket. The daemon assigns a random ID to a request that omits one, and a response is matched only against a pending request with that ID on the same connection. A dropped connection ends every command in flight on it with `outcome_unknown`. After reconnecting, only new requests are accepted.

61.content: Commands for one session run in order, and different sessions run concurrently. The extension also queues per session and answers `busy` past 32 waiting commands. `close_session` and `dialog` run outside the session queue, on a reserve of 16 slots, so a stuck session or an open dialog can still be cleared. Page CDP connections keep the protocol multiplexing: a Fetch or Debugger continuation runs while another command on the same target waits.

62.content: The default timeout is 30 seconds and the maximum is 120 seconds. A request that passes its deadline returns `outcome_unknown`, and the SDK does not retry an uncertain command.

63.content: Chrome runs the extension background as an MV3 service worker. The worker keeps one WebSocket to the daemon, sends a ping every 20 seconds, and closes the socket after 45 seconds without traffic. A `chrome.alarms` timer fires every 30 seconds and reconnects when the worker was stopped. Retries back off from 0.5 seconds to 30 seconds with jitter. No offscreen document, silent audio or polling loop keeps the worker alive, and Chrome may still stop it at any point.

64.content: A debugger session survives the worker that opened it and stays attached to its tab. The next worker starts without the state that answers paused requests. On startup it detaches the debugger sessions it inherited from the previous worker, which releases any request paused there, and attaches again on the next command. Session metadata lives in `chrome.storage.session` rather than in worker globals. Page CDP sessions end with the daemon connection that opened them.

65.content: Firefox runs an MV3 event page, which the browser suspends after 30 seconds idle. WebSocket traffic does not count as activity, so the 20-second heartbeat also calls `tabs.query` while a connection is open. A 30-second alarm reconnects after a suspension. Reloading the background drops the `webRequest` listeners and the frame selection. Presets are installed again on that tab's next controlled navigation.

66.content: The daemon is reachable only from the machine it runs on, and the token is the only credential.

67.content: It binds `127.0.0.1:17373` and rejects a request whose Host is not `127.0.0.1`.

68.content: Web origins are rejected. Only `chrome-extension://` origins with 32 letters from a to p and `moz-extension://` origins with a UUID are accepted, and only on `/extension`, `/ping` and `/pair`.

69.content: The CLI and the SDK send the token as `Authorization: Bearer`. The extension sends it as a WebSocket subprotocol, `omw-token.<token>`, next to `omw.v1`. No token appears in the URL.

70.content: `GET /ping` reports the version without a token. `POST /pair` requires an extension origin and redeems the six-digit code for the token.

71.content: A pairing code is valid for 5 minutes and 5 attempts.

72.content: The config directory is created with mode 0700. `config.json`, which holds the token, is written to a temporary file and published atomically with mode 0600.

73.content: The token grants full control of the browser: page JavaScript in any tab, raw CDP, and file writes to the absolute paths you name. It does not isolate you from another process running as the same OS user, and the profile's cookies are available to every tab.

74.content: The Chrome extension has no `<all_urls>` host permission, no resident content script and no external message entry point. Firefox declares `<all_urls>`, which screenshots, request filtering, cookies and cross-origin frames need; `userScripts` stays optional and is granted in the setup page or under **Settings**, then **Pages**.

75.content: These are capacity guards, not a bound on RSS: concurrent screenshots and Chrome's own tab and network caches still add memory.

172.content: The Firefox build is an MV3 extension for Firefox 153 and later. It pairs with the same daemon and exposes the same actions as the Chrome extension, with the differences listed under Actions. Where the Chrome extension uses CDP, the Firefox extension uses WebExtension APIs: page actions run in a content script, presets, network capture and extra request headers use blocking `webRequest` listeners, screenshots use `tabs.captureTab`, and `evaluate` uses `userScripts`.

Upload the unsigned `.xpi` in the AMO Developer Hub, or run `web-ext sign --channel=unlisted --api-key=<JWT issuer> --api-secret=<JWT secret>` in the extracted directory. `web-ext` writes the signed `.xpi` to `web-ext-artifacts/`.

184.content: AMO validates each submission before it signs it. Signing can take up to 24 hours, and each version needs its own signature.

186.content: Installing the extension opens the setup page (`app.html`), which lists the setup steps:

187.content: **Start the daemon**: `omw start`, or `omw service install` to start at login. The step completes when the page reaches the daemon.

188.content: **Pair this browser**: run `omw pair`. It prints a six-digit code that is valid for 5 minutes and 5 attempts. Type it into the pairing code field.

190.content: **Try it with an agent**: `omw install-skill ~/.agents/skills`, then ask the agent something.

191.content: **Access to all websites** is the `<all_urls>` host permission, requested at installation. You can turn it off under Permissions in `about:addons`. Without it, page actions, `screenshot` and `cookies` return `restricted_tab` and presets stop filtering requests. A `navigate` to a URL that answers 204 No Content or 205 Reset Content then waits until the command deadline. Turning the permission back on restores filtering.

192.content: **User scripts** is the optional `userScripts` permission. Choose **Allow scripts** in step 3, or under **Settings**, then **Pages**, and confirm the Firefox prompt. Firefox accepts the request only from a user action, so these buttons are the only place to grant it. Until it is granted, `evaluate` and `wait` with `expression` return `unsupported`.

193.content: **Pause** in the popup disconnects the extension from the daemon until you select **Resume**.

194.content: The daemon keeps one Chrome connection and one Firefox connection at the same time. A second connection from the same browser gets HTTP 409.

195.content: A command with `browser` goes to that browser: `omw call --browser firefox SESSION ACTION` on the command line, `connect(session, { browser: "firefox" })` in the SDK.

196.content: A command without `browser` goes to the browser the session is bound to. An unbound session goes to the only connected browser, or to Chrome when both are connected.

197.content: The first command the daemon sends binds the session to that browser. Bindings are stored in `bindings.json` and survive extension reconnects and daemon restarts.

198.content: `browser` naming the other browser returns `session_browser` (HTTP 409). A bound browser that is not connected returns `browser_offline`; the daemon does not move the session to the other browser. `close_session` removes the binding.

199.content: `/json`, `/json/list`, `/json/version` and `/devtools/page/*` use Chrome. With only Firefox connected they return `unsupported` (HTTP 501).

200.content: `omw status` and `omw doctor` print one connection line for each browser.

224.content: A Firefox extension cannot produce trusted input. `click`, `dblclick`, `mouse_click`, `hover` and `send_keys` dispatch `pointer*`, `mouse*` and `key*` events with `isTrusted` set to `false`. The page gets no user activation. Popups from `window.open`, file choosers, fullscreen and clipboard reads that the page starts from these events fail. `click` still calls `element.click()` afterwards, which runs the default action of links, buttons and form controls. `fill` and `key_type` use `document.execCommand` and produce trusted `beforeinput` and `input` events. `hover` does not set `:hover`, so a menu that opens from CSS `:hover` stays closed. `send_keys` accepts `Backspace`, `Delete`, `Enter`, `Tab`, `Shift+Tab`, `Control+A` and `Meta+A`. Other keys return `unsupported`.

225.content: The background runs as an MV3 event page. Firefox suspends an idle event page after 30 seconds, and WebSocket traffic does not count as activity. While the extension is connected it sends a ping every 20 seconds and calls `tabs.query`, which keeps the page loaded. An alarm every 30 seconds reconnects after a suspension. Session metadata lives in `storage.session`, which Firefox clears when it restarts.

491.content: Chrome DevTools Protocol access through the daemon, in extension and native mode.

499.content: The daemon exposes Chrome DevTools Protocol in two modes at `127.0.0.1:17373`, the same address and port as the rest of its API:

500.content: **Extension mode** serves page targets through `chrome.debugger` in the Chrome extension. It needs a paired Chrome extension and works with the browser profile you already have open.

501.content: **Native mode** is a WebSocket proxy to a Chrome browser endpoint you start with remote debugging. It is enabled with `omw serve --cdp`.

502.content: Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, including WebSocket upgrades. Get the token with `omw connection`. The `Host` header must be `127.0.0.1`. Requests that carry a web `Origin` are rejected with 403.

503.content:
| Endpoint              | Method | Reply                                   |
| --------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `/json`, `/json/list` | GET    | The open page targets, as a JSON array. |

504.content:
| Endpoint        | Method | Reply                                             |
| --------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `/json/version` | GET    | A version object without a browser WebSocket URL. |

505.content:
| Endpoint                 | Method    | Reply                        |
| ------------------------ | --------- | ---------------------------- |
| `/devtools/page/{tabId}` | WebSocket | One CDP session for one tab. |

506.content: When only the Firefox extension is connected, these endpoints answer HTTP 501 with the error code `unsupported`. When no browser is connected, `/json` and `/json/list` answer HTTP 503, while `/json/version` still returns its object.

507.content: `id` is the tab id. The list covers non-incognito HTTP(S) and `about:blank` tabs that belong to sessions and tabs you opened, because the extension can attach to both.

508.content: The object has no `webSocketDebuggerUrl`, so a client that discovers targets through `/json/version` finds none in this mode.

509.content: Connect to `ws://127.0.0.1:17373/devtools/page/{tabId}` with the Bearer header on the upgrade request. Before the WebSocket is accepted, the daemon asks the extension to attach to that tab.

510.content: A tab another session is using answers HTTP 409 and is not taken over.

511.content: The tab is released when the client disconnects, when the tab closes, when the debugger detaches, and when the daemon stops or the extension pauses or disconnects. Clients can reconnect afterwards.

512.content: Events for the tab are subscribed before the attach starts, so events that arrive before the attach reply are still forwarded.

513.content: Messages use the CDP shape. Commands need `id` and `method`:

514.content: A reply carries `result`, or an error object with code `-32000`:

515.content: Events carry `method`, `params` and, when the event belongs to a child target, `sessionId`. Replies can arrive out of order; the original ids are preserved.

518.content:
| Limit                | Value      |
| -------------------- | ---------- |
| Deadline per command | 30 seconds |

520.content: An event larger than 32 MiB is not forwarded. The bridge emits `Inspector.detached` for that tab and closes the connection. The daemon also closes the connection for an event whose parameters exceed 256 KiB. A client that cannot keep up with the event stream is disconnected rather than silently losing events.

521.content: When the page reports `Inspector.detached` without a `sessionId`, the daemon forwards it and closes the WebSocket, which matches the behavior of Chrome's own page endpoint.

522.content: The `cdp` action sends one protocol command on the session's current tab, attaching the tab if needed. It is the same transport as a page connection, without the WebSocket.

523.content:
| Argument | Type     | Meaning                                       |
| -------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `method` | `string` | Protocol method, for example `Page.navigate`. |

524.content:
| Argument | Type     | Meaning                              |
| -------- | -------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `params` | `object` | Method parameters. Defaults to `{}`. |

525.content:
| Argument    | Type     | Meaning                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sessionId` | `string` | Child target session, for a flat session opened by `Target.attachToTarget` with `flatten: true`. Omitted, the command goes to the tab's root session. |

526.content: The action is available in Chrome only. Firefox answers `unsupported` with HTTP 501 and the message `cdp is not available in Firefox: Firefox has no Chrome DevTools Protocol`.

527.content: Two methods interact with the rest of the bridge:

528.content: `Page.disable` on the root session clears the `@e` references of that tab. The next `snapshot` or `navigate` enables Page events again.

529.content: `Runtime.disable` ends the frame selection of that session. Later commands run in the main frame until `frame` selects one again.

530.content: The URL must start with `ws://` or `wss://` and include a host. Otherwise the daemon refuses to start. Start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` to get that URL from `http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version`.

531.content: In native mode, `/json/version` adds the browser WebSocket URL and reports the other transport:

532.content: `/devtools/browser` opens a WebSocket to that URL and copies frames in both directions, so every CDP domain and every browser-level target is available. It answers HTTP 503 while native mode is not configured (501 while only the Firefox extension is connected), and HTTP 502 when the configured endpoint cannot be reached. The upstream dial has a 10 second timeout.

533.content: Playwright can connect to the proxy:

534.content: Set `OMW_TOKEN` to the `token` value from `omw connection`. Playwright reads `/json/version` and uses the `webSocketDebuggerUrl` it finds.

535.content: Native mode does not replace extension mode. `/json/list` still lists targets through the Chrome extension, so without the Chrome extension it answers HTTP 503 (501 while only the Firefox extension is connected) even when the proxy works.

536.content: Extension mode carries page targets only. The browser target endpoint is not available, and the domains Chrome allows to `chrome.debugger` are a subset of the full protocol. See the `chrome.debugger` reference for that list.

537.content: Native mode forwards whatever the configured endpoint accepts; the daemon does not filter domains or methods.

538.content: Chrome does not accept `--remote-debugging-port` together with the default profile directory in current versions. Point it at a separate user data directory; see remote debugging.

539.content: CDP replies, events and the `cdp` action's result share the 32 MiB message limit of the rest of the bridge. The action's arguments, like any `/command` body, are limited to 2 MiB.

660.content: A session is the unit of work in oh-my-webbridge. Every command names a session, and the daemon routes it to the tabs that session holds. Tabs opened by a session sit in a tab group titled with the session name or the title the agent passed, so a task's pages stay together and apart from the pages you use.

661.content: Give each task its own session name and reuse it for everything the task does. Tasks that run at the same time use different names. Each session keeps its own tabs, tab group, current tab, presets and frame selection. The browser runs commands from different sessions at the same time.

662.content: A session starts with its first command. Its name is 1 to 96 letters (including CJK), digits, `_`, `.` or `-`.

663.content: A session's first command decides the browser it stays in: the browser named by `browser`, the only connected browser, or Chrome when both are connected. 664.content: Each session has one queue. Commands for a session run one at a time, in the order the daemon receives them, so a click that follows a snapshot acts on the page that snapshot described. A background restart drops the `webRequest` listeners and the frame selection:
A blocked top-level page leaves the tab on its current page, with no error page.
A chip in the bottom right corner with an orange dot and the session name.

A command from an agent or a script runs in your ordinary Chrome or Firefox profile, so pages keep that profile's logins, cookies and extensions. The daemon runs on the same computer as the browser and listens only on `127.0.0.1:17373`.

A command may carry a `browser` field. A session binds to a browser on its first command and keeps that binding until `close_session` succeeds. The binding is written to `bindings.json`, so after a daemon restart the session is routed back to the same browser. The next hello re-reports the session names, and stale bindings are dropped.
A command with `browser` goes to that browser: `omw call --browser firefox SESSION ACTION` on the command line, `connect(session, { browser: "firefox" })` in the SDK.
A command without `browser` goes to the browser the session is bound to. An unbound session goes to the only connected browser, or to Chrome when both are connected.
